name: Adam Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good afternoon, Adam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential. Is it all right to begin?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, of course. I'm not sure I'll be very interesting, but I'll try.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You don't need to be interesting, just honest. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Japanese and English for small import companies. A tea importer, a kitchenware firm and a company that brings in garden tools. Mostly it's contracts, product sheets and long emails back and forth with suppliers in Japan. Twice a year I interpret at the trade fair at the convention centre, standing next to a buyer for three days. I work from a desk in the spare room, with my paper dictionaries, which my girlfriend Clara laughs at.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I trust them. I know where things are on the page. I'm slower than the other translators I know, and I still check every contract twice because I'm afraid of getting a clause wrong. The tea importer pays me a monthly retainer, which is unusual and lucky, because Mr Tanaka, the owner, likes that I phone him instead of just emailing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds fine. That sounds like what I'd hope for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, people still need translators who understand business. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really post. I'd mention it to Clara over dinner and that would be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not fully. The kitchenware firm already started running its supplier emails through a free machine translator last spring, and they send me fewer. If even the boring bit gets automated, that's my steady filler work going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am, and try to keep the tea importer happy, because the retainer is the core of my income. I'd wait and see what the kitchenware firm does before I do anything. Maybe I'd ask the garden tool company if they need more help with their catalogue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm on the surface, a bit uneasy underneath. I don't like small things changing without me noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your income is the tea importer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About half. Mr Tanaka pays a fixed amount each month and I do whatever he needs. If my client Mr Tanaka ever retired or sold the business, I'd lose half my income in one phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the free machine translator do to the kitchenware work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They used to send me maybe twenty emails a week. Now it's five or six, the hard ones. I earn less, but the work I get is more interesting, so I can't say I'm completely unhappy.

say: People still need translators who **understand business**.
I don't really post; I'd just mention it to **Clara** over dinner.
think: The kitchenware firm already uses a **free machine translator** for emails.
Even a plateau takes my **filler work**, the routine emails.
do: **Keep going** exactly as now and keep the tea importer happy.
**Wait and see** what the kitchenware firm does next.
Ask the garden tool company about **catalogue work**.
feel: **Calm** on the surface, a bit uneasy underneath.
S0.quote: If my client Mr Tanaka ever retired or sold the business, I'd lose half my income in one phone call.
fieldNote: Half his income rests on **one loyal client** and a retainer.
He's a **quiet, careful** person who doesn't post or campaign.
He has already seen **routine emails** move to a free tool.

steps.text: Keep the tea importer's retainer by phoning Mr Tanaka weekly
Wait to see whether the kitchenware firm cuts more emails
Ask the garden tool company about catalogue translation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one sounds more likely, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business. Companies will use what's cheaper, and you can't really blame them. I'd say translators need to find where they're still useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, contracts and emails are exactly the writing and checking on that card. The kitchenware firm would stop sending anything, and the garden tools catalogue would go to a machine. I'd probably keep the tea importer while Mr Tanaka is there, because he likes the phone calls, but I'd lose maybe a third of my income within a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save more, maybe 400 a month, by eating out less. I'd ask Mr Tanaka if the tea company might take me on properly, in-house, handling the Japanese suppliers, not just translating. Otherwise I'd wait and see, because I don't want to jump into some course for a job that might also disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd sleep a bit worse. But I wouldn't feel hopeless, because I have savings and Clara has a steady job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My girlfriend Clara keeps telling me to try the AI tools, but honestly I'd feel like I was cutting off my own hand. Maybe I'd try one for the emails eventually. I'd probably put it off until I had no choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an in-house job at the tea importer actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering from the tea farms, phoning suppliers in Japan, sorting problems with shipments. Less translation, more relationships. I think I'd like it, actually, because the phone calls are my favourite part already.

I wouldn't blame the firms; **that's how it goes**.
think: Contracts and emails are exactly the **writing and checking** on the card.

The tea importer stays only while **Mr Tanaka** is there.
do: Save about **400 a month** by eating out less.

**Wait and see** rather than start a new course.

S1.quote: My girlfriend Clara keeps telling me to try the AI tools, but honestly I'd feel like I was cutting off my own hand.
fieldNote: He doesn't **blame anyone**; he sees it as plain business.
His real asset is **relationships**, especially phone calls with suppliers.
He'd **delay** using AI until he has no choice.

steps.text: Save about 400 a month by eating out less
Ask the tea importer about an in-house supplier role
Hold off on retraining until the picture is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should do something, though I'm not sure what. Probably help people retrain, something sensible. I wouldn't be marching, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose everything I do now by 2028. Contracts, emails, even the trade fair, because a little earpiece would interpret better than me. The only part left is the phone calls with Mr Tanaka, and even he would eventually use the earpiece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Tanaka straight away about the in-house job, and I'd take a warehouse and logistics role there if that's what's going, because packing and shipping is hands-on and the robots come later. I'd cut spending hard, no holiday, no new things. And I'd talk to my parents about whether they'd let Clara and me stay in their flat rent-free a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. I'm not a quick changer, and two years is quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say any of that to Clara?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to. I'd tell Clara I'm scared and that I don't know what I'm good at if it isn't languages. She'd tell me I'm good at being patient with difficult people, which is true, but you can't put that on a CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come about three years after the AI. Does a warehouse job feel like a real answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it feels like a waiting room. Three years in a warehouse, then the robots. But I'd rather be in a waiting room with a salary than at home reading my paper dictionaries for nothing.

say: The government should help people **retrain**, something sensible.
I'm **not sure** what the right answer is yet.
think: By **2028** I lose contracts, emails and trade fair work.
A small **earpiece** would interpret better than me.
do: Ask the tea importer for **any in-house job**, even in the warehouse.
**Cut spending** hard: no holiday, no new things.
Ask his **parents** to let them stay rent-free longer.
feel: Overwhelmed by speed, because he's **not a quick changer**.
S2.quote: I'd rather be in a waiting room with a salary than at home reading my paper dictionaries for nothing.
fieldNote: He sees the **warehouse job** as a waiting room, not a solution.
Family **support** matters: his parents' flat is part of his cushion.
His real strength, **patience** with people, feels unsellable to him.

steps.text: Take any in-house job at the tea importer, warehouse included
Cancel the holiday and stop buying new things
Ask his parents to keep the flat rent-free longer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit better. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should start preparing now, schools and companies both. I'd say it to friends, calmly. I wouldn't make speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still lose the translation by 2031. Five years would let me get into the tea company properly first, maybe as the person who manages the Japanese suppliers. The ordering itself is thinking work, so that goes too, but the visits and the trust take longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Tanaka this year about moving in-house over two years, while I still do some translation. I'd save harder, maybe 500 a month. And I'd take the forklift and warehouse safety course, just in case, because that's a few hundred and it's hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but less sharp. I'd feel like I had to keep checking the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A forklift course is quite a turn for a translator.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. My dad drove a forklift for twenty years and he'd find it very funny. But it's cheap, it's a week, and if everything with thinking goes, I'd like one thing on my CV that's done with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to save 500?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, mostly, and my yearly trip to Japan for the tea fair. That trip is the one thing I'd really miss.

I'd say it **calmly** to friends, no speeches.

**Save 500 a month** by cutting meals out and the Japan trip.
Take a week-long **forklift course**, just in case.

S3.quote: My dad drove a forklift for twenty years and he'd find it very funny.
fieldNote: He thinks the **relationship side** of import work outlasts the paperwork.

steps.text: Move in-house at the tea importer over two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I could live with that more easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be sensible and plan. I'd say it at the trade fair to the other interpreters, probably over lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get maybe five or six more years of translation, slowly shrinking. I'd be thirty-seven when it arrives, which is young enough to do something else. I don't have to decide this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am for now and keep the retainer. I'd wait a couple of years to see which way it goes before choosing anything. Then, around 2030, I'd move into the tea company properly or into some kind of buying role where I visit suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quietly. More like a long to-do list than a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI tools with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in a few years, if everyone else has and it's clearly fine. I'm not a first person to try things. I'm more the tenth person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job where people still want to shake my hand. Maybe in the tea trade, maybe something else. I'd like Clara and me to have a house by then, too.

I'd raise it over **lunch** with other interpreters at the trade fair.
think: I'd get **five or six** more years of shrinking translation.
At **thirty-seven** I'm young enough to do something else.
do: **Keep going** with the retainer for now.
Wait **a couple of years** before choosing a new direction.

S4.quote: I'm not a first person to try things. I'm more the tenth person.
fieldNote: With ten years he **delays** decisions, true to his nature.

steps.text: Keep the tea importer's retainer and current clients

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I don't change quickly, and two years would take everything before I'd made up my mind. What would help is some kind of short, paid training for a new job, and maybe someone to tell me honestly what I'm good at.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about trust. My clients trust me because I phone them and they hear my voice. I wonder if a machine that's always right will ever be trusted the way a slow person who's careful is.

headlineQuote: My clients trust me because I phone them and they hear my voice.
portrait: Adam is a 27-year-old **Japanese-English** translator for small import firms, working from a spare room.
Half his income is a **retainer** from a tea importer whose owner likes his phone calls.
He never uses **AI tools**, keeps paper dictionaries and prefers to wait and see.
In faster scenarios he'd move **in-house** at the tea firm, even into the warehouse.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would take everything before he'd made up his mind.
whatWouldHelp: Short, **paid training** for a new job.
Someone to tell him **honestly** what he's good at.
